content.thinking: I need to understand archive and restore flows and how comments relate to issues and projects.

I need to understand the full search behavior more carefully.

Two search bugs were identified. Archiving an issue removes it from the index but leaves its comments behind. Archiving a project removes the project itself, yet issues and comments remain searchable even when those issues were not archived.

Archiving a project must also purge all its issues and comments from the index. Future edits and comments on those issues must be blocked from indexing.

Restoring an archived project should re-index the project itself, any still-live issues, and their live comments.

Archived issues and their comments must stay hidden. Rebuilding the search index is broken: it resurrects archived issues, deleted comments, and archived project content, while older issues remain missing in large workspaces. The reindex job must leave only the entries permitted by the rules for every workspace entry, never touching other workspaces.

The reindex job is capped at 100 items per page, so large workspaces are only partially rebuilt. It indexes archived rows because the index writers always upsert without checking if an item is searchable. Stale documents are never deleted. The code comment claims the rebuild intentionally hands every row to the writers and leaves searchability decisions to them, but the writers currently ignore that check.

Search visibility is strictly hierarchical. A project is searchable only while live. An issue is searchable only when both the issue and its project are live. A comment is searchable only when the comment, its issue, and that issue’s project are all live.

Restoring a project does not restore issues that were archived with it or independently before. Those issues remain archived even after the project is restored.

Restoration does not un-archive issues; they are restored individually.

Restored projects never appear in search. Issues and comments stay hidden if archived. Live issues return to search.

The reindex job comment explains that archived rows are read during rebuilds to restore project content. Every row is passed to the index writers, and the decision of whether it should be searchable is left to them.

The reindex job must call indexIssue, indexComment, and indexProject directly. The indexing logic should live in those functions. If an entity is not searchable, it should be deleted from the index rather than upserted. For issues, indexIssue will check its own archivedAt field and look up the project's archived status to decide whether to remove or add it.

indexComment will delete archived comments, issues, or projects from the index. indexProject will delete archived projects. The reindex job still has pagination bugs: it only fetches the first page of 100 rows and must walk through all content. Stale documents that no longer exist may also survive indexing.

Deleted comments might not appear in listComments even with includeArchived. Orphan index rows could also survive. The first page of archived content gets re-indexed because the index functions always upsert. Live content beyond page 100 is skipped. Stale entries remain because rebuild never deletes them. Fixing the index functions to drop non-live content and paginating all rows including archived would ensure all live searchable content is upserted and all archived or deleted content that is walked is removed.

Orphan index entries that no longer match any current row would still survive. The rebuild must leave exactly the allowed entries for that workspace and must not touch any other workspace's entries. This means upserting all allowed documents and then deleting everything else.

Two approaches are being weighed. Clearing the entire organization index first and reindexing only live content would avoid reading archived rows, but the job comment requires archived rows to be read and searchability decisions to remain with the index writers.

Clearing the entire organization index at the start is the cleanest approach. Walking only live rows and upserting them directly produces exactly the correct set of allowed entries. Walking archived rows and relying on the index writers to delete them afterward would be redundant.

The first page of 100 rows may contain a mix of archived and live items if includeArchived is used. Because the list orders newest first, the first page re-adds recent archived entries while older live content remains unprocessed and older stale entries survive. The cleanest fix is to delete all search documents for the organization first, then paginate and index only the searchable live content.

Option B, walking all rows and deleting unseen documents afterward, is too complex. Option A is preferred because it avoids touching other organizations if deletion is scoped by orgId. The search repository currently lacks a bulk delete-all-for-org function, so one would need to be added or each document deleted individually. The existing deleteSearchDocument could handle non-searchable items, but orphaned rows would still require separate cleanup.

Orphan index entries are unlikely because comments, issues, and projects are soft-deleted rather than hard-deleted. The cleanup job only removes search documents without touching underlying rows. Index entries for subjects that no longer exist could still survive if tests insert them or if cleanup jobs delete issues.

The wipe must be scoped to the organization. Event listeners need four rules. Archiving an issue removes it and its comments. Archiving a project removes it and all its issues and comments. Restoring a project reindexes only live issues and their comments. Issue creation or updates are indexed only when the issue and project are both live.

Comment creation must be gated by the live status of the comment, its issue, and its project. The search.reindex_requested handler currently only processes issues and needs to cover comments and projects too. The reported bug occurs because comments posted on archived issues are still indexed.

The issue.updated handler must verify project liveness before upserting. If the project is archived, it should remove the issue from the index instead of reindexing it.

Status and assignee changes do not trigger reindex because they do not alter the searchable title and description fields.

Comment body edits currently emit no events, so those changes never update the search index.

Checking issue filters by project ID, archive methods for projects, and comment listing by organization.

The reindex job needs pagination loops until nextCursor is null. The includeArchived flag returns both archived and live issues in createdAt descending order, so the first page captures only the newest 100 items and older issues are skipped.

Archived issues, comments, and projects are being reindexed because the upsert logic never removes them. indexIssue must skip archived issues and check their parent project. indexComment and indexProject must remove archived records instead of re-upserting them.

Walking every project, issue, and comment would reconcile all index rows. Orphan entries remain if the source is deleted after indexing. Tests may create these orphans via direct upserts.

A bug in includeArchived could hide rows from the list, leaving orphan index entries behind. The safest approach is to delete all search_index rows for the organization first, then rebuild the index.

Walking only live projects, issues, and comments is sufficient if the index is wiped first. Archived records do not need to be enumerated separately. The job must call indexIssue, indexComment, and indexProject directly rather than reimplementing their logic.

Tests may spy on the index functions, so the deletion logic should live inside indexIssue, indexComment, and indexProject rather than in the job itself. Wiping all organization documents first is safe: archived items will be deleted harmlessly, and live items will be upserted correctly.

A dedicated `deleteSearchDocumentsForOrg` helper will be added to the search repository. It will run at the start of reindex to purge every document for that organization without touching other orgs. A more precise alternative would query existing rows and delete only those outside the allowed set, but that requires building the allowed set first. The race risk from live writes is acceptable because this is a background job.

Archiving an issue removes its document and all related comments. Archiving a project removes the project, its issues, and their comments. Restoring a project requires re-reading each issue to determine whether it is live or archived; archived issues and their comments must not be indexed. The restore event does not include this state.

Issue indexing should only occur when both the issue and its project are live. Archived or non-searchable issues must be removed from the index, and their comments must not be added later.

A comment is indexed only if the comment, its issue, and the project are all live. Deletion is already handled.

The `search.reindex_requested` listener currently processes only issues. It should also handle comments and projects based on the event type. Nothing emits this event for comments yet, so the edit bug likely stems from `issue.updated` alone.

Comment edits currently bypass search indexing entirely, so updated comment bodies remain stale. The fix is to emit `search.reindex_requested` from `updateComment` so the listener reindexes the comment. The listener must also handle comment events.

Project updates do not emit events, so project name edits would not refresh search either. The rule likely requires the visibility invariant to hold across archiving and restoring, rather than demanding that every edit update content.

Live issue title edits already propagate correctly via `issue.updated`. The real gaps are archived projects: live issues and comments under an archived project remain searchable, which violates the visibility rule. Comment creation must also be blocked when any ancestor is archived. For comment body edits, the existing index entry still satisfies the rule as long as the old text matches the live comment.

Scope is being limited to the four reported support issues. Comment and project edit reindexing will be left out to avoid expanding beyond the described problems.
